passages.title: Cue-elicited craving and the limits of extinction
paragraphs: In classical conditioning a stimulus that reliably precedes a biologically significant event comes to elicit a response of its own. Investigators applied this framework to appetite. One hundred twenty adults who reported eating sweet snacks most days completed 20 acquisition trials in a small testing room. On each trial a 500 ms tone sounded, and three seconds later a sweetened snack was delivered through a chute. Immediately after each tone, and before the snack arrived, participants rated how strongly they wanted the snack on a scale from 0 to 100.

Participants were then assigned at random to one of three groups of 40 for a second phase. The standard extinction group received 20 trials on which the tone sounded and no snack followed, in the same room used for acquisition. The context-change extinction group received the same 20 tone-alone trials, but in a differently furnished room on another floor. The no-extinction group spent the same length of time in the acquisition room completing unrelated questionnaires and received no tone at all. Group sizes were equal and no participant was told that the second phase differed from one group to another.

All participants returned the next day and were tested with five tone-alone trials in the original acquisition room, and again two weeks later under the same conditions. Mean craving ratings at each stage are given in Table 1. No snack was delivered on any trial after the acquisition phase, and the research assistant who collected the test-day ratings did not know which group a participant had been in. Each value in Table 1 is the mean of a participant's ratings at that stage, taken on the same 0 to 100 scale throughout.

The investigators concluded that extinction had suppressed the conditioned craving without abolishing the association that produced it, and that the suppression was tied to the place in which it had been learned.

figure.caption: Table 1  Mean craving rating (0 to 100) by group and stage.

passages.title: Dividing attention in a visual search task
paragraphs: Attention is often modelled as a limited pool of capacity drawn on by whatever a person is doing. A research group tested the model with a task in which 80 adults searched a display of 16 letters for a single target letter and pressed one of two keys to report whether it was present. Reaction time was recorded from the onset of the display, and an error was any wrong key press. The 16 letters were redrawn in a new arrangement on every trial, and the target was present on half of the trials, so a participant could not succeed by guessing.

Each participant completed the search task under three conditions, in a counterbalanced order. In the single-task condition they searched the displays alone. In the low-load condition a recorded voice read two digits before each display, which participants recalled after responding. In the high-load condition the voice read six digits. Digit lists were drawn at random and the digit recall itself was scored. Mean reaction times, error rates and digit recall are given in Table 1.

A subset of 24 participants returned for five further sessions of the high-load condition. By the fifth session their mean reaction time in that condition had fallen to 760 ms, with errors at 5%, while their single-task reaction time was unchanged at 615 ms. Participants in this subset described the search as having become something they no longer had to think about, although their reports were not scored. The group noted that this subset's single-task time had not differed from the whole sample's at the first session, so the improvement under load was not a matter of these participants having been faster to begin with.

passages.title: A staged collision and the information that follows it
paragraphs: Memory for an event can be altered by information encountered after it. To examine how far that alteration depends on delay, investigators showed 150 participants a 90-second video of a cyclist and a car meeting at a junction. In the video the cyclist rides past a yield sign before entering the junction. The junction, the sign and both vehicles are visible throughout the clip, and a separate group of 20 viewers asked only to name the sign identified it correctly on every occasion.

Twenty minutes later each participant read a 200-word summary described as the account of another witness. Half the participants read an accurate summary. The other half read a summary identical in length and style except for one sentence, which stated that the cyclist had ridden past the stop sign. Participants were allocated to the accurate or misleading summary according to the order in which they arrived at the laboratory, and were allocated at random to one of two delays before testing: ten minutes or one week.

Testing used a 24-item forced-choice recognition test, one item of which asked which sign the cyclist had passed. The proportion of participants choosing the stop sign is given in Table 1. A further probe asked participants, for each item they had answered, whether they remembered seeing the detail in the video, remembered reading it in the summary, or had worked it out. Among those who chose the stop sign after the misleading summary, 68% reported having seen it in the video. Both delay groups were tested in the same room and by the same procedure, and no participant was told that the summaries differed from one participant to another.

figure.caption: Table 1  Percentage of participants choosing the stop sign, by summary and delay.

passages.title: Detection and discrimination across the adult lifespan
paragraphs: Sensory performance can be described by an absolute threshold, the weakest stimulus a person detects on half of the occasions it is presented, and by a difference threshold, the smallest change in a stimulus a person can tell apart from the standard. A research group measured both in 60 adults, 20 in each of three age bands, all of whom reported no history of ear disease.

Auditory absolute thresholds at 4 kHz were measured in a sound-attenuating booth with an adaptive procedure that raised the tone after a miss and lowered it after a hit. Sensitivity in noise was then measured with 200 trials of a faint tone presented in continuous noise, the tone being present on half the trials. The group computed d', an index of how far the signal and noise distributions are separated, and recorded the false-alarm rate, the proportion of tone-absent trials on which a participant reported a tone. Each value in Table 1 is the mean of three separate runs of the procedure, and no participant wore a hearing aid during testing.

In a third task participants lifted two containers in turn and said which was heavier. With a standard of 100 g, the group recorded the mean smallest difference each band could detect. Weber's law holds that this difference threshold is a constant fraction of the standard rather than a constant amount, so a heavier standard should require a proportionally larger difference. All three measures are given in Table 1. The containers were identical in size and surface, so only their mass distinguished them, and the order in which the pair was lifted was alternated across trials.

passages.title: Appraisal, cortisol and performance under evaluation
paragraphs: Whether a demand provokes a stress response is held to depend on how the person sizes it up: a demand judged to exceed one's resources is appraised as a threat, while the same demand judged to be within them is appraised as a challenge. Investigators tested whether appraisal could be steered by instructions. Ninety adults performed five minutes of serial subtraction aloud in front of two evaluators who gave no feedback and who did not know which instructions a participant had received.

Participants were assigned at random to three groups of 30. The threat group was told that the task measured a fixed ability and that most people fail it. The challenge group was told that the task was demanding but that effort reliably improves performance. The neutral group was told only to work as accurately as possible. Saliva was collected at baseline and at 10, 30 and 60 minutes after the task began, and assayed for cortisol. Mean values are shown in Figure 1. Samples were assayed in a single batch by a technician who did not know which group any sample came from.

Self-reported anxiety on a 1 to 7 scale after the task was 5.4 in the threat group, 4.3 in the neutral group and 3.6 in the challenge group. Arithmetic accuracy ran in the opposite direction: 61% correct in the threat group, 70% in the neutral group and 78% in the challenge group. The three groups did not differ in baseline cortisol, in age or in self-reported sleep the previous night. Serial subtraction was chosen because it is demanding, can be scored exactly, and cannot usefully be rehearsed in advance.

figure.caption: Figure 1  Mean salivary cortisol (nmol/L) at baseline and 10, 30 and 60 minutes after the task began. Solid line, threat group; dashed line, neutral group; dotted line, challenge group.

passages.title: Unanimity and dissent in a line-judgement task
paragraphs: A classic question in social psychology is how often a person will endorse a judgement they can see is wrong because everyone around them has endorsed it first. Investigators seated each of 160 participants in a group of five, the other four being confederates, and asked the group to say aloud which of three comparison lines matched a standard line in length. The participant always answered fifth. Each group completed 18 trials, and on 12 of them, chosen in advance, the confederates all named a line that was clearly the wrong length. The three comparison lines differed in length by at least 15% and were presented at the same distance from every seat in the room.

Participants were assigned at random to one of four conditions of 40. In the public unanimous condition the four confederates gave the same wrong answer and the participant answered aloud. In the correct-dissenter condition one confederate named the right line before the participant answered. In the different-wrong-dissenter condition one confederate named a wrong line other than the majority's. In the private condition the confederates were unanimous but the participant wrote the answer on a card seen by no one else.

The outcome was the percentage of the 12 critical trials on which the participant gave the majority's wrong answer, shown in Table 1. In an interview afterwards, 71% of those who had conformed in the public unanimous condition said they had seen which line matched but had not wanted to be the only person in the room disagreeing. Participants were debriefed at the end of the session and told that the other four members of their group had been working to a script.

passages.title: Message quality, personal relevance and vaccination intention
paragraphs: Models of persuasion distinguish two routes to attitude change. On the central route a person weighs the content of the argument, and the strength of that content decides the outcome. On the peripheral route the person relies on cues outside the argument, such as the number of reasons offered or the appeal of the speaker. Which route operates is held to depend on how motivated and able the person is to think about the message.

Four hundred adults were assigned at random to a 2 × 2 design. Argument quality was varied by giving either a strong message, in which each claim about a seasonal vaccine was supported by named evidence, or a weak message of the same length, in which the claims were supported only by assertion and anecdote. Personal relevance was varied by telling participants either that the vaccine was under consideration for their own age group, or that it was under consideration for an age group they did not belong to. Intention to accept the vaccine was reported on a 1 to 7 scale immediately afterwards. Participants were recruited from a standing online panel and were told only that the study concerned health communication.

Mean intention is given in Table 1. Wording was counterbalanced within each cell so that half of each group read the message phrased as a gain and half as a loss; that variation produced a small overall difference, 4.9 against 4.6. Two weeks later participants reported intention again. In the high-relevance strong-argument cell the mean was 5.6, while in the two low-relevance cells the means had converged at 4.5. No participant was offered or given a vaccine as part of the study. Attrition by the two-week follow-up was 7% and did not differ across the four cells.

figure.caption: Table 1  Mean intention to accept the vaccine (1 to 7) immediately after the message.

passages.title: Moving districts, identity and school engagement
paragraphs: Identity is formed in part by comparison with the people around us, so a change in the surrounding group is a natural occasion to study it. A longitudinal survey followed 1,200 adolescents in one metropolitan region from age 13. Over the following two years 300 of them changed school district, most often because a parent changed job or because the household could no longer meet its rent; 900 remained in the same district. The researchers refer to the two groups as movers and stayers.

At baseline and again two years later, participants completed scales of self-esteem, of identity exploration, which asks how actively a person is trying out ways of describing themselves, and of school engagement, which asks about attention in class, homework completion and participation in school activities. All three were scored from 1 to 5. Mean scores are given in Table 1. Forty participants, half from each group, also gave an interview. All three scales had been used in earlier waves of the same survey and were administered in the same order on each occasion.

In the interviews, movers more often described keeping track of two sets of expectations, those of the friends they had left and those of the people they now saw daily, and several said they presented themselves differently to each. Stayers rarely described anything of the kind. The researchers note that the groups were not formed by random assignment and that the circumstances prompting a move may themselves affect the outcomes measured. Attrition over the two years was 9% overall and was slightly higher among movers than among stayers.

passages.title: Explaining another person's job loss
paragraphs: People explain behaviour by appealing either to something about the person or to something about the situation, and the balance they strike depends on whose behaviour is being explained. A survey experiment put the question to 600 adults living in one city. Each respondent read a 150-word account of an adult who had lost a job when a workplace reduced its staff. The accounts were identical except for one detail, assigned at random: the person was described either as living in the respondent's own neighbourhood or as living in a distant neighbourhood of the city. The sample was recruited to match the city's distribution of age, sex and household income, and each respondent read only one version of the account.

Respondents then chose whether the loss was due mainly to the person's own shortcomings or mainly to circumstances beyond their control, and rated their confidence. Afterwards, respondents were asked whether they had ever lost a job themselves. The 190 who said they had were asked, in the same sitting, to say what had caused their own loss using the same two options.

The percentage attributing a loss mainly to the person's own shortcomings is given in Table 1. The research team also recorded, for each respondent, whether they would be willing to have the person in the account as a neighbour, and 17% of those reading about the distant neighbourhood said they would prefer not to, against 6% of those reading about their own neighbourhood. The account named no employer and gave no detail of the person's work history beyond length of service.

passages.title: Two districts of one metropolitan region
paragraphs: Populations change through births, deaths and movement, and the three can be read off a district's vital statistics. A regional statistical office published figures for two districts of the same metropolitan region, which are served by the same national health insurance scheme and the same regional government. Northvale is an older, wealthier district of long-standing housing. Southmere has grown quickly on the edge of the region and houses a much younger population.

The office reported, for one calendar year, the crude birth rate and crude death rate per 1,000 residents, net migration per 1,000 residents, the share of the population under 15 and aged 65 or over, and the number of physicians practising per 10,000 residents. These are given in Table 1. The office notes that the two districts had almost identical total populations in the year reported. Rates are expressed per 1,000 residents of the district in which the events occurred, using the mid-year population as the denominator.

A second report broke Northvale's own population into fifths by household income. Life expectancy at birth was 82 years in the richest fifth and 74 years in the poorest fifth. Because both fifths hold the same insurance entitlement and live within the same district boundary, the report argues that entitlement alone cannot account for the eight-year gap, and points instead to differences in housing, in working conditions, in the food available nearby and in the stress of making ends meet. Neither district contains a large institutional population such as a prison or a university hall of residence, which can distort an age structure.
